09-098.r: Rock Edict I → bans animal sacrifice and festive gatherings (samaja); fits this question, though the book prints Pillar Edict V, which lists protected animals.
09-098.c: Rock Edict I bans animal sacrifice and festive gatherings (samaja), exactly what the question describes, as the book's own quote shows. So (a) is the better answer; Pillar Edict V lists protected animals.

09-099.r: Sohgaura copper plate (Gorakhpur, UP; Mauryan) → earliest royal order to store food-grains for famine; Mahasthan inscription (Bogura, Bangladesh) also records famine relief.

09-100.r: Ashoka annexed Kalinga because it controlled land and sea routes to South India and overseas trade; A and R both true, R explains A.

09-101.r: Mauryas gave no land grants on religious basis (A true); no peasant revolt against grants is recorded (R false). Earliest religious land-grant record → Satavahana inscription.

09-102.r: Megasthenes → Greek ambassador of Seleucus Nicator at Chandragupta Maurya's court (fourth century BC); wrote 'Indica'.

09-105.r: Megasthenes' Indica → Mauryan society in seven classes: philosophers, farmers, herdsmen, artisans-traders, soldiers, overseers (spies), councillors; also says India had no slavery.
09-105.t: Seven classes is Megasthenes' view, not the four-varna system.

09-109.r: Megasthenes (Indica) → Indian philosophers were of two kinds: Brahmins and Shramanas.

09-110.r: Mauryan tax evasion → death penalty (Indica). Pataliputra had a 30-member council of six committees of five; the sixth collected sales tax.

09-111.r: Megasthenes' Indica → describes Pataliputra's city administration: six committees of five members each; town officials called 'Astynomoi'.
09-111.h: Six committees x five members ran Pataliputra.

09-117.r: Registration of births and deaths → municipal function continuing since Mauryan times; Megasthenes' third city committee kept these records; city head 'Nagrak' or 'Purmukhya'.

09-118.r: Kautilya's rural units, ascending → Samgrahana (10 villages), Karvatika (200), Dronamukha (400), Sthaniya (800).
09-118.c: Answer not printed; book says the question is incorrect as no option gives this ascending order.

09-119.r: Mauryas developed culture, art and literature, provincial divisions (five provinces in Ashoka's inscriptions) and rule up to the Hindukush; gold coins were regularised by Indo-Greek kings.
09-119.t: Gold coins are not a Mauryan feature; credit Indo-Greeks (and later Kushanas).

09-120.r: Bhaga and Bali → sources of revenue; Bhaga = king's share of land produce (king owned the land, per Arthashastra).

09-121.r: Sitadhyaksha → head of crown agricultural land, dealt with land revenue; Shulkadhyaksha → trade and service taxes; Akradhyaksha → mines; Agronomoi → district officers.

09-122.r: Sita (Mauryan period) → revenue from crown land, managed by the Sitadhyaksha.

09-123.r: Vivit (Vivita) → tax on pastures in Mauryan India; pasture-land officer = Vivitadhyaksha.

09-124.r: Samaharta → revenue collection in the Mauryan ministerial council; Antapal → border forts; Pradeshtha → administrator of commissionaries.

09-125.r: Pautavadhyaksha → weights and measures; Panyadhyaksha → commerce; Sitadhyaksha → agriculture; Sunadhyaksha → slaughterhouse.

09-126.r: Agronomai (Mauryan) → construction of roads (UPPSC answer); they also collected revenue, watched irrigation and did legal work.
09-126.t: Not weights and measures (that is Pautavadhyaksha).

09-127.r: Pankodakasannirodhe → Mauryan penalty for slushing the road (letting dirt, silt or water collect on roads).

09-128.r: Talar → officer of night guards; Pattakola → village tax collector; Sahsadhipati → officer for dacoity cases; Baladhip → guard of octroi.

09-129.r: Taxila (now in Punjab, Pakistan) → most famous centre of learning in the Mauryan period; Nalanda grew in the Gupta period.
09-129.t: Don't pick Nalanda: its first Buddhist temples came in Gupta times.

09-130.r: Arthashastra's two courts → Dharmasthiya (civil cases) and Kantakshodhana (criminal cases).

09-131.r: Maagadha → professionals who memorised chronicles, dynastic histories and epic tales.

09-132.r: Governing villages through autonomous elected panchayats → evolved by the Dravids (Cholas); base of village administration then.

09-133.r: Arthashastra → allows divorce and remarriage to a wife deserted by her husband; husband too could leave a barren or adulterous wife.

09-134.r: Manusmriti → prohibits widow remarriage; a widower could remarry.
09-134.t: Arthashastra, by contrast, allows divorce and remarriage.

09-135.r: Manusmriti → foreigners (Shakas, Kushanas, Hunas) who did not follow priestly customs were called 'Fallen Kshatriyas'.

09-136.r: Order of visits → Megasthenes (Chandragupta Maurya), Fa-Hien (Chandragupta II), Hiuen-Tsang (Harshavardhana), I-Tsing (7th century AD).

09-137.r: Chandragupta → Sandrocottus; Bindusara → Amitraghat (Amitrachates); Ashoka → Piyadasi; Chanakya → Vishnugupta.
09-137.h: Amitraghat = 'slayer of foes', Bindusara's Greek-recorded title.

09-138.r: Cholagangam Lake → Rajendra I; Dharma Mahamatras → Ashoka; Assembly at Prayag → Harshavardhana; Sudarshan Lake → Chandragupta Maurya.

09-139.r: Last Mauryan emperor → Brihadratha, assassinated by his commander Pushyamitra Shunga in 185 BC, who founded the Shunga dynasty.

09-140.r: Brihadratha (last Maurya) killed by commander Pushyamitra Shunga; last Shunga Devabhuti killed by minister Vasudeva Kanva; last Kanva Susharma deposed by Andhra Simuk. All correct.
09-140.h: Maurya → Shunga → Kanva → Andhra: each was ended by its own servant.

09-141.r: Pranayam (Pranay) → emergency tax in the Mauryan period.

09-142.r: Girnar water management → Chandragupta Maurya (governor Pushyagupta built Sudarshan Lake) and Ashoka (governor Tushasp dug canals); both recorded in Rudradaman's Junagadh inscription.
09-142.t: Rudradaman repaired the lake centuries later, not 'before the Christian era'.

09-145.r: Junagadh rock (near Uparkot fort) → carries Ashoka's fourteen edicts, Rudradaman I's inscription and Skandagupta's inscription; tells the Sudarshan Lake story.

09-146.r: Barabar caves (Jahanabad, Bihar) → four caves, Ashoka's inscriptions on three, given to Ajivakas (founded by Makkhali Gosala); Mauryan, not 6th century BC.

09-147.r: Mauryan Manibhadra Yaksha idol → found at Parkham near Mathura; now in Mathura museum.

09-148.r: Correct: Lothal → ancient dockyard; Sarnath → Buddha's first sermon; Nalanda → Buddhist learning. Wrong: Ashoka's Lion Capital is at Sarnath, not Rajgir.

09-149.r: Vishakhadatta's play Mudrarakshasa → court intrigues in the time of Chandragupta Maurya.

10-001.r: Strato II (Indo-Greek ruler, c. 25 BC-10 AD) → issued lead coins.

10-002.r: Agathocles (Greco-Bactrian, c. 190-180 BC) → silver coins showing Sankarshana (Balram) and Vasudeva; first bilingual coin legends (Greek and Brahmi).

10-003.r: Milinda (Menander, Indo-Greek) → not a contemporary; Bimbisara, Gautama Buddha and Prasenjit (Koshala) were contemporaries.

10-004.r: Earliest specimen of Sanskrit Kavya style → Junagadh (Girnar) inscription of Rudradaman (130-150 AD), in Brahmi script, perfect Sanskrit.

10-005.r: Junagadh inscription (Sanskrit, c. 150 AD) → achievements of Rudradaman I: patron of arts and Sanskrit; repaired embankments of the Mauryan Sudarshana lake.

10-006.r: Rudradaman I → renovated Sudarshan Lake without forced labour (Junagadh inscription); lake first built by Chandragupta Maurya's governor Pushyagupta.

10-007.r: Junagadh Sanskrit inscription (second century CE) → Rudradaman I repaired Sudarshan Lake, an artificial reservoir built by Chandragupta Maurya.

10-008.r: Kardamaka Kshatrapas → silver coins common, potin coins also; copper coins very rare (Chastana issued silver and copper).

10-009.r: Demetrius → Indo-Greek; Rudradaman → Scythian (Shaka); Gondophernes → Parthian; Vima → Kushana.

10-010.r: Invaders of ancient India in order → Greeks, Sakas, Kushanas.
10-010.h: GSK (like the drug company): Greeks, Sakas, Kushanas.

10-011.r: Kushanas → issued the largest number of copper coins in north and north-west India and issued gold coins regularly; Indo-Greeks first issued gold coins there.

10-013.r: Buddha is depicted on the coins of Kushana ruler Kanishka.

10-014.r: Vima Kadphises → first Kushana ruler to issue gold coins (Indo-Greek rulers had made gold coins popular earlier).

10-015.r: Vima Kadphises (father of Kanishka I) → introduced gold coins for regular use, on a large scale; Kujul Kadphises circulated copper coins.
10-015.h: Kujula = copper (first king), Vima = gold (second king).

10-017.r: Vima Kadphises (Kadphises II, father of Kanishka I) → took the title 'Sarvalokeshvara' (Lord of the Whole World).

10-018.r: Yaudheya copper coins → six-headed God Kartikeya standing, with a peacock.

10-019.r: Kanishka's Sarnath Buddha image inscription → dated 81 AD, three years after his coronation (78 AD).

10-020.r: Kanishka's coronation → 78 AD, agreed at the London conference of 1960 (after 1913); start of Saka Samvat.

10-021.r: Saka Samvat → began 78 AD; Sakas beat Vikramaditya's successor in 135 Vikrama Samvat (135 - 57 = 78); Kanishka generally credited as its founder.

10-022.r: Difference between Vikrama Samvat (57 BC) and Saka Samvat (78 AD) → 135 years.

10-023.r: Chaitra 1 of the Saka-based national calendar → 22 March (21 March in a leap year).
